results.construction: Drag the handles to (0,-1) and (2,3), both on y=2x-1, or equivalently (-1,-3) and (2,3). The gradient is 2 and the intercept is -1. Both are lattice points within the grid, and the start positions (-3,-2) and (1,1) are not a problem in equation mode.

predicates.why: It fires on a line with gradient 1/2 (run over rise), for example through (0,-1) and (2,0). A student who computes Δx/Δy from the equation or from points would draw exactly this. It is in the equation-mode can_emit list.

It fires on a line with gradient -2, for example through (0,-1) and (1,-3). The question gives the equation directly, so there is no coordinate subtraction for the stated mechanism to act on. A student who draws -2 here has most likely misread or mishandled the sign, or the 'negative' in the printed '+ -1', rather than subtracted in the wrong order. The diagnosis would mostly serve a refutation of a mistake she did not make.

results.construction: Equation mode with y = -x + 3: drag the two handles to (0,3) and (3,0). Both are lattice points within the grid, and the line through them has gradient -1 and intercept 3. Other valid pairs: (1,2) and (2,1), or (-2,5) and (4,-1).

predicates.why: The reciprocal of -1 is -1, so inverting the slope gives the correct line. The predicate cannot fire for this question, and a student who inverted the slope would be marked correct.

It fires for the line y = x + 3, built from (0,3) and (1,4), which has the right intercept and magnitude but the wrong direction. A student who plots 3 on the y-axis and then goes up 1 and right 1 instead of down 1 makes exactly this error.

results.construction: Equation mode: drag handles to lattice points (0,0) and (2,2). The line through them is y = 1x + 0, so it is accepted. Any two points on y=x work, e.g. (-2,-2) and (3,3). The points-mode handle restriction does not apply.

predicates.why: The reciprocal of m=1 is 1, so the inverted line is the same as the correct line. The predicate can't fire on a wrong answer here, and it can't separate this misconception from a correct answer.

It would fire on y = -x (through (0,0) and (2,-2)). But the rule is given directly as y = 1x + 0, with no two points to subtract. A student with the 'subtract in opposite order' misconception has nothing to compute, so a sign flip here is more likely a slip or misreading than that misconception.

results.construction: Equation mode, m=-2, b=2. Drag handles to lattice points (0,2) and (1,0); the line through them is y=-2x+2 (also (-1,4) and (2,-2) work). All within limits: |m|=2<=5, b=2 in -5..5.

predicates.why: Fires on a line with gradient -1/2 (reciprocal), e.g. through (0,2) and (2,1). A student who takes run over rise from -2 builds exactly this, keeping the intercept 2.

Fires on gradient +2 with intercept 2, e.g. through (0,2) and (1,4). A student who drops or misapplies the minus sign on -2x draws the rising line, so the sign was lost while the steepness stayed right.

results.construction: x+2y+2=0 gives y=-x/2-1, so m=-1/2 (reciprocal of -2, allowed) and b=-1 (in range). Drag one point to (0,-1) and another to (2,-2) (or (-2,0)). Both are lattice points on the line. The y-axis part from the origin has length 1.

predicates.why: A student who writes m=a/b=1/2 instead of -1/2 and uses intercept -1 draws y=x/2-1. That has the right magnitude and the opposite sign, so the predicate fires. It is the misconception's signature.

A student who reads the coefficients without isolating y takes m=1 and b=2, or m=2. The line y=x+2 has neither the right slope nor the right intercept, so off-target fires. This is the typical product of the misconception.

This fires when the slope is -1/2 but the intercept is wrong. A student who got -1/2 must have isolated y, so she would normally have the intercept right too. A wrong intercept there is more likely a sign or arithmetic slip, such as b=+1. Reading coefficients without isolating y gives a wrong slope, so this predicate mostly fires for other reasons.

results.construction: Equation mode: drag points (0,2) and (2,3). Both satisfy x-2y+4=0 (slope 0.5, intercept 2). Neither is at the default handle positions (-3,-2) or (1,1). The limits hold: |m| = 0.5 = 1/2, b = 2 in -5..5.

predicates.why: A student who writes m = a/b = 1/(-2) = -0.5 instead of -a/b draws a line with slope -0.5, the sign-flipped version of the correct slope. This is exactly the claimed misconception.
A student who reads the coefficient of x as the slope (1) and the constant as the intercept (4) draws y = x + 4. Neither the slope nor the intercept matches, so off-target fires for this error.

This needs slope 0.5 with an intercept other than 2. A student who reads the constant straight off without isolating y also gets the slope wrong, because the x coefficient is 1, not 1/2. A correct slope with a wrong intercept would mostly come from an arithmetic slip, not from this misconception. Attributing it to this misconception would be wrong.

results.construction: Rearranged: y = -2x + 3. Equation mode, so drag the two handles to lattice points (0,3) and (2,-1) (avoiding the opening handle spots (-3,-2) and (1,1), though (1,1) is on the line). Slope -2, y-intercept 3 (length 3). Within limits: |m|=2, b=3.

predicates.why: Fires on y = 2x + 3 (e.g. points (0,3),(1,5)): correct magnitude, wrong sign, correct intercept. A student using m = a/b = 2 instead of -a/b = -2 would build exactly this, while still finding the intercept 3.

Fires on slope -2 with an intercept other than 3. A student who reads coefficients straight off 2x + y - 3 = 0 gets slope +2 (not -2), so they would not keep the correct slope; this construction would come from a different error.
Reading the coefficients without isolating y gives m = 2 and b = -3, i.e. y = 2x - 3 (e.g. (0,-3),(1,-1)). Neither slope nor intercept matches, so off-target fires and fits this misconception.
